{{short description|Type of planar curve with tree-like structure}}
[[File:Tree-like curve.svg|thumb|upright=1.2|A tree-like curve with finitely many marked double points]]
In [[mathematics]], particularly in [[differential geometry]], a '''tree-like curve''' is a [[General position|generic]] [[immersion (mathematics)|immersion]] <math>c: S^1 \to \mathbb{R}^2</math> with the property that removing any [[double point]] splits the curve into exactly two [[disjoint sets|disjoint]] [[connected component (topology)|connected components]]. This property gives these curves a [[tree (graph theory)|tree]]-like structure, hence their name. They were first systematically studied by Russian [[mathematicians]] [[Boris Shapiro]] and [[Vladimir Arnold]] in the 1990s.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Aicardi | first = F.
 | editor-last = Arnol'd | editor-first = V. I.
 | contribution = Tree-like curves
 | isbn = 0-8218-0237-2
 | location = Providence, Rhode Island

 | title = Singularities and bifurcations
 | volume = 21
 | year = 1994}}</ref><ref name="Shapiro-1997">{{citation
 | last = Shapiro | first = Boris
 | editor-last = Tabachnikov | editor-first = S.
 | arxiv = dg-ga/9708009
 | contribution = Tree-like curves and their number of inflection points
 | doi = 10.1090/trans2/190/08
 | isbn = 0-8218-1354-4
 | location = Providence, Rhode Island
 | mr = 1738394
 | pages = 113–129
 | publisher = American Mathematical Society
 | series = American Mathematical Society Translations, Series 2
 | title = Differential and symplectic topology of knots and curves
 | volume = 190
 | year = 1999}}</ref>

For generic curves interpreted as the shadows of [[Knot theory|knots]] (that is, [[knot diagram]]s from which the over-under relations at each crossing have been erased), the tree-like curves can only be shadows of the [[unknot]]. As knot diagrams, these represent [[connected sum]]s of [[Lemniscate|figure-eight curves]]. Each figure-eight is unknotted and their connected sum remains unknotted. Random curves with few crossings are likely to be tree-like, and therefore random knot diagrams with few crossings are likely to be unknotted.<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Cantarella | first1 = Jason
 | last2 = Chapman | first2 = Harrison
 | last3 = Mastin | first3 = Matt
 | doi = 10.1088/1751-8113/49/40/405001
 | issue = 40
 | journal = Journal of Physics
 | mr = 3556174
 | article-number = 405001
 | title = Knot probabilities in random diagrams
 | volume = 49
 | year = 2016| arxiv = 1512.05749
 }}</ref>
